claim: The striatum is critically involved in value-based decision making.
source: The striatum is critically involved in value-based decision making.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Balleine et al., 2007; Hikosaka et al., 2006; Ito and Doya, 2011; Lee et al., 2012; Macpherson et al., 2014) as indicated in the Introduction.

claim: Value-based decision making consists of two distinct steps: value-based action selection and value updating based on choice outcomes.
source: value-based decision making, which consists of two distinct steps: value-based action selection and value updating based on choice outcomes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Direct-pathway SPNs project directly to the endopeduncular nucleus (EP) and the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr).
source: In rodents, direct-pathway SPNs project directly to the endopeduncular nucleus (EP; homologous to the globus pallidus interna in primates) and the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smith et al., 1998.

claim: Indirect-pathway SPNs project indirectly to the EP/SNr via the globus pallidus (GP) and subthalamic nucleus.
source: indirect-pathway SPNs project indirectly to the EP/SNr via the globus pallidus (GP) and subthalamic nucleus (Smith et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smith et al., 1998.

claim: Direct-pathway striatal neurons selectively express D1 receptors (D1R).
source: Direct-pathway striatal neurons selectively express D1 receptors (D1R)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gerfen et al., 1990.

claim: Indirect-pathway striatal neurons express D2 receptors (D2R).
source: whereas indirect-pathway striatal neurons express D2 receptors (D2R) (Gerfen et al., 1990)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gerfen et al., 1990.

claim: The segregation of D1R and D2R expression is less strict in the ventral striatum.
source: although such a segregation is less strict in the ventral striatum (Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smith et al., 2013.

claim: mCherry was expressed in the dorsal striatum and EP in D1R-Cre mice.
source: Histological examinations after completion of behavioral experiments revealed that mCherry and eGFP were expressed in the dorsal striatum and EP in D1R-Cre mice
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and described in the text based on histological examination.

claim: mCherry was expressed in the dorsal striatum and GP in D2R-Cre mice.
source: Histological examinations after completion of behavioral experiments revealed that mCherry and eGFP were expressed in the dorsal striatum and EP in D1R-Cre mice and in the dorsal striatum and GP in D2R-Cre mice
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and described in the text based on histological examination.

claim: The expression patterns confirm selective expression in direct- or indirect-pathway SPNs.
source: confirming their selective expression in direct- or indirect-pathway SPNs, respectively (Figure 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical expression patterns shown in Figure 1.

claim: All animal groups learned to choose the rewarding target during the initial 3 days of training (stage 1).
source: All animal groups learned to choose the rewarding target (either left or right; counterbalanced across animals) during the initial 3 d of training (stage 1).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from the reversal task.

claim: All animal groups learned to choose the other rewarding target after reversal over 4 days of training (stage 2).
source: After reversal of the rewarding target, all animal groups learned to choose the other rewarding target over 4 d of training (stage 2).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data from the reversal task.

claim: Performances of the three animal groups were similar during across-session reversal (stage 3).
source: Performances of the three animal groups were also similar during across-session reversal (reversal of the rewarding target at the beginning of each daily session; stage 3; two-way between-groups ANOVA, main effect of mouse line, F(1,46) = 2.8, p = 0.101; main effect of animal group, F(2,46) = 2.04, p = 0.141; mouse line × animal group interaction, F(2,46) = 0.15, p = 0.858).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data from stage 3 of the reversal task.

claim: Performance of the CNO group was significantly lower compared with other animal groups in stage 4.
source: However, performance of the CNO group was significantly lower compared with other animal groups in stage 4 (main effect of mouse line, F(1,46) = 3.64, p = 0.063; main effect of animal group, F(2,46) = 58.54, p = 2.3 × 10−13; mouse line × animal group interaction, F(2,46) = 3.58, p = 0.036; post-hoc Bonferroni test, D1R-Cre mice, CNO vs. DMSO, p = 9.9 × 10−8, CNO vs. eGFP-CNO, p = 2.1 × 10−8, DMSO vs. eGFP-CNO, p = 0.089; D2R-Cre mice, CNO vs. DMSO, p = 0.003, CNO vs. eGFP-CNO, p = 3.6 × 10−5, DMSO vs. eGFP-CNO, p = 0.326)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data from stage 4 of the reversal task.

claim: Performance of the CNO group was significantly lower compared with other animal groups in stage 5.
source: and stage 5 (main effect of mouse line, F(1,46) = 0.11, p = 0.747; main effect of animal group, F(2,46) = 39.32, p = 1.1 × 10−10; mouse line × animal group interaction, F(2,46) = 0.05, p = 0.954; post-hoc Bonferroni test, CNO vs. DMSO, p = 2.1 × 10−8, CNO vs. eGFP-CNO, p = 2.9 × 10−9, DMSO vs. eGFP-CNO, p = 0.195; Figure 2b,c)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data from stage 5 of the reversal task, shown in Figure 2.

claim: The performance deficits following D1R or D2R neuronal inactivation could not be attributed to differences in trial duration across animal groups.
source: However, further analysis revealed that the performance deficits following D1R or D2R neuronal inactivation could not be attributed to differences in trial duration across animal groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on additional analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inactivation of D1R- or D2R-expressing striatal neurons impairs reversal learning.
source: Having established that inactivation of D1R- or D2R-expressing striatal neurons impairs reversal learning and that this is not attributable to a nonspecific effect of CNO using separate groups of animals
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral results in the reversal task.

claim: Animal choice behavior in the dynamic TAB task was well captured by the Q-learning model.
source: Consistent with this finding, animal choice behavior in this task was well captured by the Q-learning model, a simple reinforcement learning model (Sutton and Barto, 1998) (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is based on model fitting to behavioral data, shown in Figure 3a.

claim: There was a significant main effect of drug without a significant mouse line × drug interaction effect on P(R) in the TAB task.
source: We found a significant main effect of drug without a significant mouse line × drug interaction effect on P(R) (two-way mixed-design ANOVA, main effect of mouse line, F(1,37) = 6.214, p = 0.017; main effect of drug, F(1,37) = 32.636, p = 1.5 × 10−6; mouse line × drug interaction, F(1,37) = 0.530, p = 0.471)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data from the TAB task.

claim: There was a significant main effect of drug without a significant mouse line × drug interaction effect on P(H) in the TAB task.
source: as well as P(H) (main effect of mouse line, F(1,37) = 4.020, p = 0.052; main effect of drug, F(1,37) = 31.591, p = 2.1 × 10−6; mouse line × drug interaction, F(1,37) = 0.0004, p = 0.984; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data from the TAB task, shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Inactivating either D1R- or D2R-expressing striatal neurons impairs performance in the TAB task.
source: These results indicate that inactivating either D1R- or D2R-expressing striatal neurons impairs performance in the TAB task.
evidence: This is inferred from the statistical results showing main effects of drug on P(R) and P(H).

claim: There was a significant mouse line × drug interaction effect on P(R) in the dynamic state.
source: In the dynamic state, we found a significant mouse line × drug interaction effect on P(R) (two-way mixed-design ANOVA, main effect of mouse line, F(1,37) = 6.719, p = 0.014; main effect of drug, F(1,37) = 14.76, p = 4.6 × 10−4; mouse line × drug interaction, F(1,37) = 4.5128, p = 0.040)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data from the dynamic state of the TAB task.

claim: CNO significantly decreased P(R) in D2R-Cre, but not D1R-Cre, mice in the dynamic state.
source: Post-hoc Bonferroni tests revealed a significant CNO effect on P(R) in D2R-Cre, but not D1R-Cre, mice (p = 1.8 × 10−4 and 0.226, respectively; Figure 3c).
evidence: This is based on post-hoc statistical tests of behavioral data from the dynamic state, shown in Figure 3c.

claim: There were significant mouse line × drug interaction effects on P(H) and P(LS) in the steady state.
source: In the steady state, we found significant mouse line × drug interaction effects on P(H) (main effect of mouse line, F(1,37) = 0.009, p = 0.926; main effect of drug, F(1,37) = 9.0145, p = 0.005; mouse line × drug interaction, F(1,37) = 5.1513, p = 0.029) and P(LS) (main effect of mouse line, F(1,37) = 0.853, p = 0.362; main effect of drug, F(1,37) = 2.9786, p = 0.093; mouse line × drug interaction, F(1,37) = 8.735, p = 0.005)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data from the steady state of the TAB task.

claim: CNO significantly decreased P(H) in D1R-Cre, but not D2R-Cre, mice in the steady state.
source: Post-hoc Bonferroni tests revealed significant CNO effects on P(H) and P(LS) in D1R-Cre, but not D2R-Cre, mice (P(H), p = 5.6 × 10−4 and 0.612 in D1R-Cre and D2R-Cre mice, respectively
evidence: This is based on post-hoc statistical tests of behavioral data from the steady state.

claim: CNO significantly decreased P(LS) in D1R-Cre, but not D2R-Cre, mice in the steady state.
source: P(LS), p = 0.002 and 0.396, respectively).
evidence: This is based on post-hoc statistical tests of behavioral data from the steady state.

claim: CNO significantly decreased P(WS) in D1R-Cre, but not D2R-Cre, mice in the steady state.
source: CNO effect on P(WS) was significant in D1R-Cre, but not D2R-Cre, mice (p = 2.6 × 10−4 and 0.273, respectively; Figure 3c).
evidence: This is based on post-hoc statistical tests of behavioral data from the steady state, shown in Figure 3c.

claim: CNO significantly increased the randomness in action selection in D1R-Cre, but not D2R-Cre, mice.
source: We found that CNO significantly increased the randomness in action selection (or decreased value-dependent action selection) in D1R-Cre, but not D2R-Cre, mice (two-way mixed-design ANOVA, main effect of mouse line, F(1,37) = 0.398, p = 0.532; main effect of drug, F(1,37) = 8.8886, p = 0.005; mouse line × drug interaction, F(1,37) = 7.2601, p = 0.011; post-hoc Bonferroni test, CNO vs. DMSO, D1R-Cre mice, p = 2.4 × 10−4, D2R-Cre mice, p = 0.842).
evidence: This is based on Q-learning model parameter estimation from behavioral data.

claim: CNO significantly decreased learning rate in D2R-Cre, but not D1R-Cre, mice.
source: We also found that CNO significantly decreased learning rate in D2R-Cre, but not D1R-Cre, mice (main effect of mouse line, F(1,37) = 1.303, p = 0.261; main effect of drug, F(1,37) = 6.4289, p = 0.016; mouse line × drug interaction, F(1,37) = 5.9142, p = 0.020; post-hoc Bonferroni test, CNO vs. DMSO, D1R-Cre mice, p = 0.941, D2R-Cre mice, p = 0.001; Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on Q-learning model parameter estimation from behavioral data, shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The findings regarding learning rate and randomness in action selection were consistent across several variants of the Q-learning model.
source: These results were consistent across several variants of the Q-learning model containing additional parameters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; see Supplementary file 1 for results of model comparisons).
evidence: This is based on additional model analyses shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inactivation of D1R-expressing striatal neurons selectively impairs value-dependent action selection.
source: Collectively, these findings indicate that inactivation of D1R-expressing striatal neurons selectively impairs value-dependent action selection
evidence: This is inferred from the model-based analysis showing increased randomness in action selection without changes in learning rate.

claim: Inactivation of D2R-expressing striatal neurons selectively impairs value learning.
source: and inactivation of D2R-expressing striatal neurons selectively impairs value learning.
evidence: This is inferred from the model-based analysis showing decreased learning rate without changes in randomness in action selection.

claim: The mean Qhigh value in the dynamic state was significantly smaller in CNO compared with DMSO sessions in D2R-Cre, but not D1R-Cre, mice.
source: Qhigh changed more slowly after block transition in CNO than DMSO sessions such that the mean Qhigh value in the dynamic state was significantly smaller in CNO compared with DMSO sessions in D2R-Cre, but not D1R-Cre, mice (two-way mixed-design ANOVA, main effect of mouse line, F(1,37) = 12.133, p = 0.001; main effect of drug, F(1,37) = 5.5095, p = 0.024; mouse line × drug interaction, F(1,37) = 14.147, p = 5.8 × 10−4; post-hoc Bonferroni test, CNO vs. DMSO, D1R-Cre mice, p = 0.318, D2R-Cre mice, p = 1.3 × 10−4; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is based on analysis of action values derived from the Q-learning model, shown in Figure 4b.

claim: No significant effect of CNO was found on Qlow after block transition.
source: No significant effect of CNO was found on Qlow after block transition (main effect of mouse line, F(1,37) = 0.299, p = 0.588; main effect of drug, F(1,37) = 0.2265, p = 0.637; mouse line × drug interaction, F(1,37) = 0.2891, p = 0.594; Figure 4b)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of action values derived from the Q-learning model, shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The lack of CNO effect on Qlow suggests preferential contributions of striatal D2R-expressing neurons to learning from positive outcomes.
source: suggesting preferential contributions of striatal D2R-expressing neurons to learning from positive outcomes (Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Fiorillo, 2013) (see also Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects on Qhigh vs. Qlow and supported by citations.

claim: Qhigh and Qlow were similar between CNO and DMSO sessions in the steady state in D1R-Cre as well as D2R-Cre mice.
source: As expected, Qhigh and Qlow were similar between CNO and DMSO sessions in the steady state in D1R-Cre as well as D2R-Cre mice (Qhigh, main effect of mouse line, F(1,37) = 4.881, p = 0.033; main effect of drug, F(1,37) = 0.54679, p = 0.464; mouse line × drug interaction, F(1,37) = 0.57919, p = 0.452; Qlow, main effect of mouse line, F(1,37) = 1.786, p = 0.190; main effect of drug, F(1,37) = 0.64447, p = 0.427; mouse line × drug interaction, F(1,37) = 0.41336, p = 0.524; Figure 4c).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of action values in the steady state, shown in Figure 4c.

claim: D1R neuronal inactivation decreases the degree of value-dependent action selection without affecting learning rate.
source: We found D1R neuronal inactivation decreases the degree of value-dependent action selection without affecting learning rate
evidence: This is a summary of the model-based analysis results.

claim: D2R neuronal inactivation decreases learning rate without affecting value-dependent action selection.
source: whereas D2R neuronal inactivation decreases learning rate without affecting value-dependent action selection.
evidence: This is a summary of the model-based analysis results.

claim: Dorsal striatal direct and indirect pathways might play crucial roles in distinct stages of value-based decision making.
source: These findings suggest that dorsal striatal direct and indirect pathways might play crucial roles in distinct stages of value-based decision making.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of D1R vs. D2R neuronal inactivation.

claim: Selective effects of CNO on D1R-Cre versus D2R-Cre mice argue against non-specific effects of CNO.
source: Even though we did not test eGFP-CNO mice in the dynamic foraging task, selective effects of CNO on D1R-Cre versus D2R-Cre mice (as opposed to common CNO effects on both mouse lines) argue against non-specific effects of CNO.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of results showing differential effects between mouse lines.

claim: It is unlikely that inactivation of D1R- and/or D2R-expressing striatal interneurons contributed to the observed behavioral effects.
source: There remains a possibility that inactivation of D1R- and/or D2R-expressing striatal interneurons (GABAergic fast-spiking interneurons and cholinergic tonically active neurons) might have contributed to the observed behavioral effects. However, this is unlikely because similar, small percentages of parvalbumin-positive and choline acetyltransferase-positive striatal neurons are labeled in D1R-Cre and D2R-Cre mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; see also Shin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to Shin et al., 2018.

claim: Direct and indirect pathways may play more important roles in different domains of decision making.
source: Our results raise the possibility that direct and indirect pathways play more important roles in different domains of decision making.
evidence: This is speculated based on the current findings.

claim: Value learning is impaired in D2R-knockout mice, but not D1R-knockout mice.
source: We have shown previously that value learning is impaired in D2R-knockout mice, but not D1R-knockout mice (Kwak et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: D2R has been implicated in reversal learning.
source: There also exists a large body of literature indicating a role for D2R in reversal learning, although D1R has also been implicated in this process (Izquierdo et al., 2017; Klanker et al., 2013; Waltz, 2017).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior literature.

claim: Reversal learning is impaired by selectively inactivating striatal neurons in the indirect pathway, but not the direct pathway.
source: Reversal learning is also impaired by selectively inactivating striatal neurons in the indirect pathway, but not the direct pathway (Piray, 2011; Yawata et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior studies.

claim: Indirect pathway striatal SPNs carry stronger previous reward signals than direct pathway SPNs in mice.
source: Furthermore, indirect pathway striatal SPNs carry stronger previous reward signals than direct pathway SPNs in mice (Shin et al., 2018)
evidence: This is based on citation to Shin et al., 2018.

claim: In monkeys, striatal injection of a D2R, but not D1R, antagonist impairs learning from past outcomes.
source: and in monkeys, striatal injection of a D2R, but not D1R, antagonist impairs learning from past outcomes (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on citation to Lee et al., 2015.

claim: The current findings are consistent with a critical role of the striatal indirect pathway in mediating value learning.
source: These studies are consistent with the current findings, which suggest a critical role of the striatal indirect pathway in mediating value learning.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistency between current and prior findings.

claim: The current results are inconsistent with the proposal that direct- and indirect-pathway striatal neurons mediate learning from positive and negative outcomes, respectively.
source: It has been proposed that direct- and indirect-pathway striatal neurons mediate learning from positive and negative outcomes, respectively (Frank et al., 2007; Frank et al., 2004). Our results are inconsistent with this proposal in that inactivating D1R-expressing striatal neurons had no significant effect on learning rate.
evidence: This is based on comparison of current findings with prior theoretical proposals.

claim: Inactivating D2R-expressing striatal neurons impaired learning from positive outcomes.
source: Our results are also inconsistent with this proposal in that inactivating D2R-expressing striatal neurons impaired learning from positive outcomes.
evidence: This is based on the current findings showing effects on Qhigh.

claim: The effect of inactivating D2R-expressing striatal neurons on Qhigh was much greater than that for Qlow after block transition.
source: The effect of inactivating D2R-expressing striatal neurons on the action value for a high-reward–probability target (Qhigh) was much greater than that for a low-reward–probability target (Qlow) after block transition.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of action values shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Using models with separate learning parameters for positive and negative outcomes, a significant reduction in αp, but not αn, was found following inactivation of D2R-expressing striatal neurons.
source: Furthermore, using models containing separate learning parameters for positive and negative outcomes (αp and αn, respectively; models 3, 5 and 6), we found a significant reduction in αp, but not αn, following inactivation of D2R-expressing striatal neurons.
evidence: This is based on additional model analyses shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: D2R-expressing striatal neurons play a more important role in learning from positive than negative outcomes.
source: These results suggest that D2R-expressing striatal neurons play a more important role in learning from positive than negative outcomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects on learning from positive vs. negative outcomes.

claim: Dopamine has been proposed to play a role in gain control and modulation of corticostriatal action selection processes.
source: Dopamine has long been proposed to play a role in gain control and modulation of corticostriatal action selection processes (Beeler et al., 2010; McClure et al., 2003; Servan-Schreiber et al., 1990).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior literature.

claim: A previous modeling study proposed that tonic dopamine regulates randomness in action selection via D1R-expressing, but not D2R-expressing, striatal neurons.
source: In particular, a previous modeling study proposed that tonic dopamine regulates randomness in action selection via D1R-expressing, but not D2R-expressing, striatal neurons (Humphries et al., 2012), a suggestion consistent with our findings.
evidence: This is based on citation to Humphries et al., 2012 and comparison with current findings.

claim: Activating striatal direct and indirect pathways alters the gain of cortical motor commands.
source: A recent study has also shown that activating striatal direct and indirect pathways alters the gain of cortical motor commands (Yttri and Dudman, 2016).
evidence: This is based on citation to Yttri and Dudman, 2016.

claim: Changing the randomness in action selection (β) is equivalent to changing the gain of value-dependent action selection without altering action values.
source: Changing the randomness in action selection (β) is equivalent to changing the gain of value-dependent action selection without altering action values (see Equation 2).
evidence: This is based on the mathematical properties of the Q-learning model.

claim: Changing learning rate (α) is equivalent to changing the gain of reward prediction error (RPE)-dependent learning.
source: Likewise, changing learning rate (α) is equivalent to changing the gain of reward prediction error (RPE)-dependent learning (see Equation 1; note that RPE = R(t) – Qa(t)).
evidence: This is based on the mathematical properties of the Q-learning model.

claim: Striatal direct and indirect pathways may be involved in controlling the gain of value-based decision making.
source: Our results suggest that striatal direct and indirect pathways may be involved in controlling the gain, not only of motor commands, but also of value-based decision making.
evidence: This is speculated based on the current findings and comparison with prior work.

claim: Both D1R- and D2R-expressing SPN populations carry value and RPE signals.
source: We previously showed that both D1R- and D2R-expressing SPNs convey value and RPE signals, which would suggest their involvement in both value-dependent action selection and value-updating processes.
evidence: This is based on citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The activity of D1R- and D2R-expressing SPN populations increases and decreases, respectively, as a function of value.
source: In particular, the activity of D1R- and D2R-expressing SPN populations increases and decreases, respectively, as a function of value (Shin et al., 2018)
evidence: This is based on citation to Shin et al., 2018.

claim: Antagonistic effects of striatal D1R versus D2R (or direct versus indirect pathway SPN) manipulations on reward-based learning have been reported.
source: which fits well with the antagonistic effects of striatal D1R versus D2R (or direct versus indirect pathway SPN) manipulations on reward-based learning (Hikida et al., 2010; Kravitz et al., 2012; Nakamura and Hikosaka, 2006; Tai et al., 2012; Yawata et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior studies.

claim: Antagonistic effects of D1R- versus D2R-expressing SPN stimulation on motor behavior have been reported.
source: Likewise, antagonistic effects of D1R- versus D2R-expressing SPN stimulation on motor behavior have been reported (Durieux et al., 2012; Kravitz et al., 2010; Yttri and Dudman, 2016).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior studies.

claim: In the present study, inactivation of D1R- or D2R-expressing SPNs impaired two different aspects of value-based decision making.
source: However, in the present study, inactivation of D1R- or D2R-expressing SPNs impaired two different aspects of value-based decision making.
evidence: This is a summary of the current findings.

claim: Both direct and indirect pathways may be involved in action selection and value learning, but D1R (or D2R)-expressing SPNs alone may be sufficient to support value-dependent action selection (or value updating).
source: It may be that both direct and indirect pathways are involved in action selection and value learning, but D1R (or D2R)-expressing SPNs alone may be sufficient to support value-dependent action selection (or value updating), such that strong stimulation yields antagonistic effects whereas inactivation yields selective effects.
evidence: This is speculated as a possible explanation for the discrepancy between stimulation and inactivation studies.

claim: The direct and indirect pathways may play selective roles, and seemingly antagonistic stimulation effects are because of indirect effects of strong, potentially non-physiological, stimulation.
source: Alternatively, the direct and indirect pathways may play selective roles, and seemingly antagonistic stimulation effects are because of indirect effects of strong, potentially non-physiological, stimulation.
evidence: This is speculated as an alternative explanation.

claim: Direct and indirect pathway striatal neurons often exhibit activity that cannot be explained by a simple antagonistic or synergistic relationship between the two pathways.
source: Note that direct and indirect pathway striatal neurons often exhibit activity that cannot be explained by a simple antagonistic or synergistic relationship between the two pathways (e.g., Cazorla et al., 2014; Cui et al., 2013; Shin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior studies.

claim: Direct and indirect pathway manipulations often lead to behavioral outcomes that cannot be readily explained by their antagonistic or synergistic actions.
source: Likewise, direct and indirect pathway manipulations often lead to behavioral outcomes that cannot be readily explained by their antagonistic or synergistic actions (e.g., Jin et al., 2014; Vicente et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior studies.

claim: Both the dorsomedial and dorsolateral striatum were inactivated in this study.
source: Also note that we inactivated both the dorsomedial and dorsolateral striatum, which are likely to make substantially different contributions to behavioral control (Balleine et al., 2009; Ito and Doya, 2011; Khamassi and Humphries, 2012; Yin and Knowlton, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail with citations to prior work on striatal subregions.

claim: D1R- and D2R-expressing dorsal striatal neurons are indispensable for two different steps in value-based decision making.
source: Our results indicate that D1R- and D2R-expressing dorsal striatal neurons are indispensable for two different steps in value-based decision making.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the findings.

claim: Inactivation of D1R- and D2R-expressing striatal neurons selectively impairs value-dependent action selection and value learning, respectively.
source: A reinforcement learning model-based analysis indicated that inactivation of D1R- and D2R-expressing striatal neurons selectively impairs value-dependent action selection and value learning, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a main finding based on model-based analysis.

claim: Striatal direct and indirect pathways make differential contributions to two distinct steps in value-based decision making.
source: Our results suggest differential contributions of striatal direct and indirect pathways to two distinct steps in value-based decision making.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Percentages of co-labeled striatal neurons were similar between D1R-Cre and D2R-Cre mice.
source: Percentages were similar between D1R-Cre and D2R-Cre mice (Fisher's exact test, ChaT, p = 0.572; PV, p = 0.712).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The probability of choosing the lower-reward–probability target did not increase as a block transition approached.
source: As shown previously in a similar TAB task (Jeong et al., 2018), the probability of choosing the lower-reward–probability target did not increase as a block transition approached, arguing against the possibility that animals were able to estimate the time of reversal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to prior work.

claim: None of the slopes of logistic regression for Plower was significantly different from zero.
source: None of the slopes of logistic regression (solid lines) was significantly different from zero.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Animals were not able to estimate the time of reversal in the TAB task.
source: arguing against the possibility that animals were able to estimate the time of reversal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of increase in Plower before block transitions.
